claim: Blood analysis provides crucial health status information.
source: Blood is arguably the most important bodily fluid and its analysis provides crucial health status information.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The differential blood count determines the frequency of all major blood cells and is a routine measure to narrow down diagnosis in clinical practice.
source: A first routine measure to narrow down diagnosis in clinical practice is the differential blood count, determining the frequency of all major blood cells.
evidence: This describes established clinical practice.

claim: MORE analysis can identify all major blood cells in a drop of blood at rates of 1000 cells/sec without labeling, enrichment or separation.
source: In a drop of blood we can identify all major blood cells and characterize their pathological changes in several disease conditions in vitro and in patient samples.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated throughout the manuscript with experimental data.

claim: Blood is responsible for the distribution of oxygen and nutrients and is centrally involved in the immune response.
source: Blood is responsible for the distribution of oxygen and nutrients, and centrally involved in the immune response.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge.

claim: The complete blood count is a basic, routine measure in clinical practice.
source: The complete blood count, the analysis of presence and frequency of all major blood cells, constitutes a basic, routine measure in clinical practice.
evidence: This describes current clinical practice.

claim: Alterations in physical properties of blood could cause or reflect pathological conditions.
source: It is evident that the flow of blood throughout the body will be determined by its physical properties in the vasculature, and their alterations could cause or reflect pathological conditions (Lichtman, 1973; Baskurt and Meiselman, 2003; Popel and Johnson, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Whole blood rheology has not resulted in wide-spread diagnostic application, probably due to the dominant importance of erythrocytes at the expense of sensitivity to leukocyte properties.
source: Probably due to the dominant importance of erythrocytes, at the expense of sensitivity to leukocyte properties, whole blood rheology has not resulted in wide-spread diagnostic application.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of clinical adoption.

claim: Leukocyte activation, leukemia, and malaria infection lead to readily quantifiable mechanical alterations in major blood cells.
source: Various cell mechanics measurement techniques, such as atomic force microscopy (Worthen et al., 1989; Rosenbluth et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2008), micropipette aspiration (Lichtman, 1973; Lichtman, 1970; Dombret et al., 1995; Ravetto et al., 2014) or optical traps (Lautenschläger et al., 2009; Ekpenyong et al., 2012; Paul et al., 2013), have been used to show that leukocyte activation, leukemia, and malaria infection, amongst many other physiological and pathological changes, lead to readily quantifiable mechanical alterations in the major blood cells (Worthen et al., 1989; Lautenschläger et al., 2009; Schmid-Schönbein et al., 1973; Suresh et al., 2005; Rosenbluth et al., 2008; Bow et al., 2011; Gossett et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Previous proof-of-concept studies on cell mechanics have been done on few tens of specifically isolated cells.
source: These proof-of-concept studies have so far been done on few tens of specifically isolated cells.
evidence: This characterizes the limitations of prior research.

claim: RT-DC analyzes human blood without any labeling or separation at rates of 1000 cells/sec.
source: Mimicking capillary flow, we analyze human blood without any labeling or separation at rates of 1000 cells/sec.
evidence: This is a primary technical capability demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: MORE analysis can sensitively detect morphological and rheological changes of erythrocytes in spherocytosis and malaria infection.
source: We show that we can sensitively detect morphological and rheological changes of erythrocytes in spherocytosis and malaria infection, of leukocytes in viral and bacterial infection, and of malignant transformed cells in myeloid and lymphatic leukemias.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated with experimental data in the Results section.

claim: MORE analysis can sensitively detect morphological and rheological changes of leukocytes in viral and bacterial infection.
source: We show that we can sensitively detect morphological and rheological changes of erythrocytes in spherocytosis and malaria infection, of leukocytes in viral and bacterial infection, and of malignant transformed cells in myeloid and lymphatic leukemias.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated with experimental data in the Results section.

claim: MORE analysis can sensitively detect morphological and rheological changes of malignant transformed cells in myeloid and lymphatic leukemias.
source: We show that we can sensitively detect morphological and rheological changes of erythrocytes in spherocytosis and malaria infection, of leukocytes in viral and bacterial infection, and of malignant transformed cells in myeloid and lymphatic leukemias.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated with experimental data in the Results section.

claim: 50 µl of citrate-anticoagulated blood was diluted in 950 µl of measurement buffer for RT-DC measurements.
source: In order to establish the normal MORE phenotype of cells found in blood, we obtained venous, citrate-anticoagulated blood of healthy donors, of which 50 µl was diluted in 950 µl of measurement buffer with a controlled elevated viscosity, but without any additional labeling, sorting, or enrichment.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: Brightfield images of cells deformed by hydrodynamic shear stresses in the channel were obtained continuously by RT-DC.
source: Brightfield images of the cells, deformed by hydrodynamic shear stresses in the channel (Mietke et al., 2015), were obtained continuously by RT-DC (Otto et al., 2015) (see Materials and methods; Video 1).
evidence: This describes the measurement technique with supporting citations.

claim: RT-DC images revealed distinct differences in overall morphology, brightness, and amount of deformation between all major cell types found in blood.
source: These images revealed distinct differences in overall morphology, brightness, and amount of deformation between all major cell types found in blood (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RT-DC enabled continuous, real-time quantification of cross-sectional area and deformed shape at measurement rates of 100–1000 cells/sec.
source: RT-DC further enabled the continuous, real-time quantification of the cross-sectional area and of the deformed shape (see detailed description in Materials and methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) of an, in principle, unlimited number of cells at measurement rates of 100–1000 cells/sec (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the technical capability with reference to data.

claim: Size and brightness alone were sufficient for the identification of cell types in MORE analysis.
source: Notably, size and brightness alone — parameters not unlike those accessible by light scattering analysis in standard flow cytometers — were sufficient for the identification of the cell types (Figure 1D), so that deformation, as an additional and independent parameter, was available for assessing their functional changes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 1D.

claim: The identity of individual cell populations by size and brightness was established by magnetic cell sorting, controlled by fluorescence immunophenotyping, and subsequent MORE analysis.
source: The identity of the individual cell populations by size and brightness was established by magnetic cell sorting, controlled by fluorescence immunophenotyping, and subsequent MORE analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the validation method with reference to supporting data.

claim: Erythrocytes are clearly separated from other cells due to their much greater deformation and lower brightness.
source: A key feature is the very clear separation of the abundant erythrocytes (red blood cells; RBCs) from other cells as a result of their much greater deformation and lower brightness.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The clear separation of erythrocytes gives access to leukocyte properties directly in diluted whole blood without hemolysis or other separation steps.
source: This feature gives access to leukocyte properties directly in diluted whole blood, without the potentially detrimental effects of hemolysis (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3) or other separation steps, which are required for analysis with cell mechanics techniques with lower specificity and throughput, or non-continuous measurement.
evidence: This is an inference from the data showing clear separation and comparison with hemolysis effects.

claim: MORE phenotyping yielded identical results in repeated measurements of blood from the same donor with sodium citrate as an anti-coagulant and for different storage times.
source: In extensive tests of the variability of this approach, MORE phenotyping yielded identical results in repeated measurements of blood from the same donor, with sodium citrate added as an anti-coagulant and for different storage times (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), between different donors of both sexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), and blood samples taken at different times during the day (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reproducibility data in the supplementary figures.

claim: MORE analysis provided the identity and frequency of all major white blood cells as with a conventional differential blood count.
source: MORE analysis provided the identity and frequency of all major white blood cells as with a conventional differential blood count (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 1) — obtained from a single drop of blood, with minimal preparation, and within 15 min.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison data in Figure 1F and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Spherocytosis is a hereditary disease in which genetic changes cause abnormal shape and mechanical properties of erythrocytes.
source: Spherocytosis is a prototypical hereditary disease in humans in which genetic changes (here ankyrin and spectrin mutations) cause abnormal shape and mechanical properties of erythrocytes.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about the disease.

claim: Current diagnosis of spherocytosis is based on detection of abnormal cell shapes in a blood smear, followed by assessment of osmotic fragility.
source: Current diagnosis is based on the detection of abnormal cell shapes in a blood smear, followed up by assessment of the osmotic fragility quantified by Acidified Glycerol Lysis Time (AGLT) or by osmotic gradient ektacytometry.
evidence: This describes current clinical diagnostic practice.

claim: MORE analysis of blood from patients with spherocytosis revealed significantly less deformed and smaller erythrocytes than normal.
source: MORE analysis of the blood of patients with spherocytosis directly revealed significantly less deformed and smaller erythrocytes than normal (Figure 2A–C) as the functional correlate of the cytoskeletal mutation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2A-C and statistical analysis.

claim: The differences in erythrocyte deformation and size in spherocytosis are clear enough that MORE analysis can serve as a fast primary screening test.
source: The differences are so clear (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) that this analysis can serve as a fast primary and cheap screening test for spherocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference from the clear differences shown in the data.

claim: A change in RBC deformability has been implicated in malaria pathogenesis, since single cells infected by parasites have been reported to be stiffer.
source: A change in RBC deformability has also been implicated in malaria pathogenesis, since single cells infected by parasites have been reported to be stiffer (Bow et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The gold standard in malaria diagnosis is still a manual thick blood smear analysis.
source: This insight has not progressed towards clinical application and the gold standard in malaria diagnosis is still a manual thick blood smear analysis.
evidence: This describes current clinical practice.

claim: RBCs exposed in vitro to Plasmodium falciparum showed a clear, significant, and increasing reduction in deformation detectable after 4 hr.
source: We found a clear, significant, and increasing reduction in the deformation of the entire exposed RBC population detectable after 4 hr (Figure 2D–F; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time course data in the figures.

claim: Characteristic features associated with parasite maturation inside RBCs permitted direct identification of positively infected cells.
source: Inspection of the individual cell images revealed the appearance of characteristic features likely associated with the maturation of parasites inside a subset of RBCs (Figure 2D,E insets; Figure 2—figure supplement 2). These features permitted the direct identification of positively infected cells, whose relative frequency peaked at 36 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by image analysis and quantification in the figures.

claim: Overtly infected RBCs showed an even greater reduction in deformation than the entire exposed population.
source: The separate assessment of overtly infected cells showed an even greater reduction in deformation than observed in the entire exposed population (Figure 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which — extrapolating our in vitro results to the situation in vivo — relates to the possibility of clearance of stiff, infected cells from the circulation by the spleen (Cranston et al., 1984; Shelby et al., 2003).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data with inference about in vivo implications supported by citations.

claim: A bystander stiffening of exposed but non-infected cells seems involved in malaria infection.
source: However, this small fraction of stiffer cells alone cannot account for the reduced deformation of the whole population, so that a bystander stiffening of exposed but non-infected cells seems involved (Paul et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference from the data with supporting citation.

claim: Reduced membrane-cytoskeleton interactions have been correlated with elliptocytic RBCs and resistance to P.f. infection.
source: Reduced membrane-cytoskeleton interactions have previously been correlated with elliptocytic RBCs and resistance to P.f. infection (Chishti et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: 2 BP-treated RBC samples showed changes in deformation with a concurrent reduction in P.f. infectivity compared to buffer control or PA-treated RBCs.
source: Here, 2 BP-treated RBC samples showed changes in deformation (Figure 2G) with a concurrent reduction in P.f. infectivity (Figure 2H), compared to buffer control or RBCs treated with palmitic acid (PA).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 2G and 2H.

claim: Palmitoylation of RBC proteins is important for RBC morphology and infectivity of P.f.
source: Since both, 2 BP and PA readily accumulate in the membranes, but only 2 BP causes a reduction in infectivity of P.f., we suggest that palmitoylation of RBC proteins is important for RBC morphology and infectivity of P.f.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental comparison of 2BP and PA treatments.

claim: Leukocyte mechanics has not been utilized for diagnostic purposes, likely due to increased stiffness compared to RBCs and lack of convenient techniques.
source: While RBC mechanics has already been used for clinical diagnostics using rheoscopes and ektacytometers for over 40 years (Schmid-Schönbein et al., 1973; Cranston et al., 1984; Reid et al., 1976), leukocyte mechanics has not been utilized for diagnostic purposes. This is likely due to their increased stiffness compared to RBCs and a lack of convenient techniques capable of sufficiently deforming them in suspension — their physiological state.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations and knowledge of the field.

claim: Proof-of-concept studies showed that neutrophil activation leads to stiffening, in line with the pronounced actin cortex that is a hallmark of neutrophil activation.
source: For example, there have been proof-of-concept studies on the mechanical changes associated with activation of isolated neutrophils showing a stiffening, in line with the pronounced actin cortex that is a hallmark of neutrophil activation (Worthen et al., 1989; Rosenbluth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: MORE analysis of in vitro neutrophil activation in blood with fMLP showed neutrophils were less deformed and smaller within the first 15 min, followed by reversal to more deformed and larger cells.
source: MORE analysis of the in vitro neutrophil activation in blood with the bacterial wall-derived tripeptide fMLP confirmed that neutrophils were indeed less deformed and smaller within the first 15 min post fMLP treatment. Interestingly, the subsequent time-course showed a reversal to more deformed and larger cells (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time course data in the figures.

claim: The apparent Young's modulus of neutrophils increased from E = 742 ± 12 Pa to E = 853 ± 20 Pa during the first 15 min after fMLP stimulation.
source: Thus, we also calculated the apparent Young's modulus of the cells, which increased from E = 742 ± 12 Pa to E = 853 ± 20 Pa (mean ±SEM. p=0.009, n = 5) during the first 15 min, and then subsequently reverted to values statistically indistinguishable but slightly lower than before stimulation (15–30 min: E = 717 ± 9 Pa, p=0.347; 30–45 min: E = 719 ± 7 Pa, p=0.117; 45–60 min: E = 731 ± 11 Pa, p=0.465).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Such mechanical activation kinetics of neutrophils has not been reported before as the lower measurement rate of previous techniques yielded only cumulative data.
source: Such mechanical activation kinetics of neutrophils has not been reported before as the lower measurement rate of previous techniques yielded only cumulative data over the time period investigated.
evidence: This is an inference about the novelty of the findings based on knowledge of prior techniques.

claim: Blood from patients with acute lung injury of bacterial origin had larger and more deformed neutrophils compared to healthy controls.
source: Congruently, blood taken from patients with an acute lung injury (ALI) of most likely bacterial origin had larger and more deformed neutrophils compared to healthy controls (Figure 3C,E,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patient data in the figures.

claim: The same neutrophil response was found in blood samples from patients hospitalized with viral respiratory tract infections.
source: The same neutrophil response was found in blood samples from patients hospitalized with viral respiratory tract infections (RTI; Figure 3D,E,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patient data in the figures.

claim: Monocytes responded by a size increase in both RTI and ALI patients and after in vitro stimulation with S. aureus.
source: Also monocytes responded by a size increase in both RTI and ALI patients and after in vitro stimulation with S. aureus, but showed a significantly increased deformation only in viral RTI, while blood lymphocytes did not show any consistent response (Figure 3F–H; Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in the figures.

claim: In patients with acute EBV infection, both monocytes and lymphocytes showed an increase in cell size and deformation, while neutrophils showed less of a response.
source: The lymphocyte response changed when analyzing blood of patients with acute Epstein-Barr-virus (EBV) infection, which is known to also stimulate the lymphatic system, where both monocytes and lymphocytes showed an increase in cell size and deformation, while neutrophils showed less of a response (Figure 3I–L, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patient data in the figures.

claim: MORE blood analysis might be sufficiently sensitive to distinguish bacterial from viral infections by the differential response of selective blood leukocyte populations.
source: These results suggest that MORE blood analysis might be sufficiently sensitive to distinguish bacterial from viral infections, and potentially other inflammatory diseases, by the differential response of selective blood leukocyte populations.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the observed differential responses.

claim: MORE analysis of blood from patients with AML revealed less deformed cells but of about the same size compared to healthy and fully differentiated myeloid cells.
source: MORE analysis of the blood of patients with acute myeloid (AML) and lymphatic leukemias (ALL) revealed the new presence of atypical cell populations — the characteristic immature blasts not normally present in healthy donors (Figure 4A–C). Cell populations gated for AML revealed less deformed cells but of about the same size compared to healthy and fully differentiated myeloid cells (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), in line with previous results (Rosenbluth et al., 2006; Lichtman, 1970; Dombret et al., 1995; Lautenschläger et al., 2009; Ekpenyong et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patient data with supporting citations.

claim: ALL blast cells were larger in size compared to mature lymphocytes, but did not show any consistent trend in deformation.
source: ALL blast cells were larger in size compared to mature lymphocytes, but did not show any consistent trend in deformation (Figure 4D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the patient data in the figures.

claim: Mature lymphocytes, ALL blasts, mature myeloid cells, and AML blasts have increasing levels of stiffness.
source: Together these results show that mature lymphocytes, ALL blasts, mature myeloid cells, and AML blasts have increasing levels of stiffness, consistent with the composite findings of previous reports (Lichtman, 1973; Rosenbluth et al., 2006; Lam et al., 2008; Lichtman, 1970; Dombret et al., 1995; Lautenschläger et al., 2009; Ekpenyong et al., 2012; Rosenbluth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference from the data with supporting citations.

claim: The stiffness pattern in blood cancers is different from the general trend in solid tumors, where cancer cells are found to be more deformable than their healthy counterparts.
source: This is quite different than the general trend in solid tumors, where cancer cells are found to be more deformable than their healthy counterparts (Suresh, 2007; Kumar and Weaver, 2009; Guck and Chilvers, 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior research supported by citations.

claim: The differential stiffness of AML and ALL blasts has been implicated in the occurrence of leukostasis.
source: Sensibly, the differential stiffness of AML and ALL blasts, and its potential further increase with chemotherapy, has been implicated in the occurrence of leukostasis (Lam et al., 2008; Rosenbluth et al., 2008; Lam et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: By following the ALL blast population in a patient over 12 days of methylprednisolone treatment, the return to the normal morpho-rheological fingerprint of blood could be monitored.
source: Finally, by following the ALL blast population in a patient over 12 days of methylprednisolone treatment we could monitor the return to the normal morpho-rheological fingerprint of blood (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the longitudinal patient data in the figures.

claim: In pediatric ALL, the number of blasts at day eight after start of methylprednisolone treatment is predictive of the relapse rate.
source: The response to treatment is one of the most powerful prognostic in vivo markers of leukemia survival. In pediatric ALL the number of blasts at day eight after start of methylprednisolone treatment is predictive of the relapse rate (<1000 blasts/µl of blood: relapse rate 20–30%; >1000 blasts/µl of blood: relapse rate 50–80%).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about prognostic markers.

claim: MORE analysis provides at least the same information as conventional morphological analysis, but in a shorter amount of time and with smaller sample sizes required.
source: MORE analysis provides at least the same information as conventional morphological analysis, but in a shorter amount of time and with smaller sample sizes required (for a comparison between MORE analysis and conventional biomarkers, see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an inference from comparison with conventional methods.

claim: RT-DC stands out among microfluidic techniques because it can continuously monitor an unlimited number of cells.
source: Amongst the latter techniques, RT-DC stands out because it can continuously monitor an, in principle, unlimited number of cells, which enables the direct sensitive assessment of the state of all major cell types found in blood.
evidence: This is a technical capability of the method.

claim: A volume as small as 10 µl can be analyzed cell-by-cell with only dilution in measurement buffer.
source: A volume as small as 10 µl can be analyzed cell-by-cell, with only dilution in measurement buffer to adjust cell density and prevent sedimentation, but no labeling, enrichment or separation, which could otherwise cause inadvertent activation of blood cells.
evidence: This describes the technical capability and sample requirements.

claim: Cell mechanics and morphology are inherent and sensitive markers intimately linked to functional changes associated with the cytoskeleton.
source: Cell mechanics and morphology are inherent and sensitive markers intimately linked to functional changes associated with the cytoskeleton (Chimini and Chavrier, 2000; Fletcher and Mullins, 2010; Kasza et al., 2007; Patel et al., 2012; Salbreux et al., 2012) and other intracellular shape-determining and load-bearing entities (Rowat et al., 2006; Munder et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Label-free, disease-specific morpho-rheological blood signatures are a novel resource for generating hypotheses about underlying molecular mechanisms.
source: Thus, label-free, disease-specific morpho-rheological blood signatures are a novel resource for generating hypotheses about the underlying molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference about the potential applications of the method.

claim: At present, MORE phenotyping provides a sensitive, but not a very specific marker.
source: Of course, at present, MORE phenotyping provides a sensitive, but not a very specific marker.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of current limitations.

claim: The measurement buffer viscosity was adjusted to 15 mPa s at room temperature.
source: For RT-DC measurements, cells were suspended in a viscosity-adjusted measurement buffer (MB) based on 1x phosphate buffered saline (PBS) containing methylcellulose. The viscosity was adjusted to 15 mPa s at room (and measurement) temperature, determined using a falling ball viscometer (Haake, Thermo Scientific).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Measurements were carried out at a total flow rate of 0.12 µl/s with a sample flow rate of 0.03 µl/s and a sheath flow rate of 0.09 µl/s.
source: Measurements were carried out at a total flow rate of 0.12 µl/s with a sample flow rate of 0.03 µl/s and a sheath flow rate of 0.09 µl/s unless stated otherwise.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Images of the cells in the channel were acquired in a region of interest of 250 × 80 pixels at a frame rate of 2000 fps.
source: Images of the cells in the channel were acquired in a region of interest of 250 × 80 pixels at a frame rate of 2000 fps.
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters.

claim: All studies complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and involved written informed consent from all participants or their legal guardians.
source: All studies complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and involved written informed consent from all participants or their legal guardians.
evidence: This describes the ethical compliance of the research.

claim: Ethics for experiments with human blood were approved by the ethics committee of the Technische Universität Dresden.
source: Ethics for experiments with human blood were approved by the ethics committee of the Technische Universität Dresden (EK89032013, EK458102015), and for human blood and LPS inhalation in healthy volunteers by the East of England, Cambridge Central ethics committee (Study No. 06/Q0108/281 and ClinicalTrialReference NCT02551614).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the research.
